doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Tone as one's voice, and Raul Johnson's constant sound
summary: He argues sound is already in your head, citing Raul Johnson, son of Sun Johnson, and how players are known by their tone.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Yeah man. I think that has to do with the concept — first of all I think the sound is already there, no matter what you play on, it’s in your head. And that’s what I try — no matter what, if I’m playing somebody’s instrument I’m trying to hear that and that’s the way I’m going to hear it. I have some friends of mine, one guy in particular was a saxophone player, he comes from a family of saxophone players. His name is Raul Johnson. His father was Sun Johnson, and he was a great alto player from the Swing Era and had a great sound. He played with my dad. And I used to hear Raul play, no matter what type of mouthpiece, reed or whatever, or horn, he would always sound the same. So it made me to believe that the sound is already here. But it makes it a little easier if you have the right type of instrument man, you know, to get what you’re trying to get. But tone is everything. To me the tone of your instrument is just like your voice. We know people by just listening to the sound of their voice, just the way we know musicians from the sound of their tone of their instrument. When you hear a couple of notes you know that’s Charlie Parker. You know that’s Clifford Brown. You know that’s John Coltrane. You know that’s Clark Terry. All those great, great musicians man. So the voice is so important because when we play that is our voice.
